BHS

You are the manager

The quality of the output is the quality of your brief. Same as onboarding a new hire.

Asking

“Write a LinkedIn post about employer branding.”

Generic. Could be any company.
You rewrite it anyway.
You conclude “AI is overrated.”

Briefing

AudienceHR heads at Malaysian SMEs
Goaldrive GEC award registrations
Anglecost of a bad employer brand
Tonedirect, no corporate filler
Length150 words, one clear CTA
Referenceour best-performing post last month

Live demo: run both prompts side by side. The gap sells the whole session.

BHS

Chat, Cowork, Code

One task — “summarise this month’s inbox conversations” — in three places.

Chat

1
You paste, it answers.
Example
Quick questions, drafting, thinking out loud.
Use when
Anything under 5 minutes.

Cowork

2
It works through your files and hands back a document.
Example
The full conversation export, analysed in one pass.
Use when
Multi-step work with real files.

Code

3
It writes the thing that does it every week.
Example
A script that produces the inbox report on a schedule.
Use when
When the task repeats forever.
BHS

Projects: stop re-explaining yourself

A Project remembers your context so every output starts on-brand.

What goes in once

  • Brand tone and writing guidelines
  • Talentbank ICP and buyer personas
  • GEC award positioning and key dates
  • Your five best-performing posts
  • Service scope and pricing tiers

What comes out every time

  1. LinkedIn post announcing this year’s award cycle
  2. Facebook carousel copy for the next career fair
  3. Five post variations from one client testimonial
  4. A month of content from three themes
BHS

Artifacts & Connectors

Artifacts are things you keep. Connectors let Claude read what you already have.

Artifacts

You can edit, download and send these.

  • A one-page employer branding proposal
  • Sales objection-handling cheat sheet
  • An interactive award scoring rubric
  • A simple ROI calculator for prospects
Connectors
  • Gmail — “Pull the last 10 emails from this employer and tell me where the deal stalled.”
  • Drive — “Find our GEC award decks and list what changed year on year.”
  • Calendar — “Which meetings this week have no prep doc?”
BHS

Skills: teach it once, use it forever

A Skill is a saved set of instructions Claude loads whenever the task comes up. Without one you re-explain the format every time. With one, the output is identical whoever runs it.

1

Talentbank Proposal

Takes any scope and formats it into your standard structure, tiers and pricing — same shape every time.

2

Weekly Inbox Analysis

Ben and Li Kiat get the same report format each week without re-prompting: themes, objections, stalled deals.

Build the first one live in the session — they will remember making it more than watching it.

BHS

Scheduled tasks: work that runs without you

Set it once. It arrives whether you remember or not.

1
Monday, 8:00am

Week ahead brief

Reads your calendar and flags every meeting with no prep doc attached.

2
Friday, 5:00pm

Quiet prospect scan

Scans the shared inbox for anyone who went silent 7+ days and drafts the follow-up.

3
Daily, 9:00am

Overnight enquiries

Summarises new enquiries and sorts them by how close they are to buying.

Each of these is a real gap in the current process — not a hypothetical.

BHS

Ground rules before you start

Two minutes now saves an awkward conversation later.

1

Check the output

It is confident even when wrong. Names, numbers and dates get verified before anything leaves the building.

2

Mind what you paste

Payroll, IC numbers, bank details and signed contracts stay out. When unsure, redact first.

3

Connectors see real data

Once Gmail or Drive is connected, it reads what your account can read. Know the scope before you approve.

4

It drafts, you decide

Nothing goes to a client, a candidate or an employer without a human reading it first.

PART 3

Builder Track

Ben and Mavis — laptops open. Everyone else, enjoy the rest of your afternoon.

BHS

Getting set up

You install it yourself. Watching someone else install it teaches nothing.

1

Install VS Code

Free, from Microsoft. This is where your files live and where you will see changes happen.

2

Install Claude Code

One command in the terminal, then sign in. If the terminal is new to you, this is the only scary part — and it lasts two minutes.

3

Open a folder and ask

“What is in this folder and what does it do?” Your first win should come inside five minutes.

Nobody watches. Everyone types.

BHS

Build something real

Rebuild your own pages. Copying a competitor’s site wholesale is a legal headache, not a shortcut.

Good first builds

  • Rebuild the GEC award landing page
  • An employer client portal mockup
  • The weekly inbox analysis dashboard
  • A one-page pitch site for a campaign

How to work with it

  • Describe the outcome, not the code
  • Ask for one change at a time
  • Look at every result before moving on
  • When it goes sideways, start fresh rather than patching

BHS

/context and /cost

Two commands that answer the two questions everyone eventually asks.

/context
“Why did it get worse after an hour?”
  • Every session has a memory limit
  • Long sessions get vague and forgetful
  • Summarise, start fresh, carry the summary over
/cost
“Is this worth running every week?”
  • Shows what the session actually used
  • Compare it against the hours it replaced
  • Run it on a real task — finance will ask
